Part C · Chapter 1

Images as numbers and convolution

Pixels, colour channels and a small filter that slides over a picture and fills a feature map that marks where a pattern appears

A picture is a grid of numbers. In this chapter a filter slides over a digit to fill a feature map, stride and padding set the map's size, and max pooling shrinks it.

The digits come from MNIST and play the part of logbook tag numbers. The shark photos are credited under the figure; their depth effect comes from a simple model, not from a measurement of Mumbai water.

You will need: NumPy arrays (0.1), the dot product (0.5) and the idea of a neuron as a weighted sum (B1).

  1. A picture is a grid of numbers
  2. Colour is three grids
  3. A filter slides over the picture
  4. Stride and padding
  5. Max pooling

A picture is a grid of numbers

Guess first. Researchers write tag numbers by hand in a logbook, and the figure uses handwritten MNIST digits to play the part of logbook digits. MNIST stores one digit as a grid with 28 rows and 28 columns. How many numbers is that for one digit, and what number would you expect for a square the pen never touched?

A pixel is one square of the grid. In this grey picture it has one number, its grey value: 0 is no ink and 255 is full ink. A digit with 28 rows and 28 columns is therefore 28 × 28 = 784 numbers, and reading a handwritten digit means doing arithmetic on those 784 numbers.

  1. Move the pointer over the digit, or tap it: the box on the right writes out the framed 5 by 5 block as numbers.
  2. Read the boxes under the picture: 664 of the 784 numbers of this digit are 0, which is 85% empty paper.
  3. Tick Shuffle the squares: the 784 numbers move to new places by one fixed random rule, the count of zeros stays 664 because shuffling only moves numbers, and you can no longer read the digit.

Move over the picture.

A digit is 784 numbers, and 664 of them (85%) are 0, the empty paper; the pen path is a thin ridge of values up to 255.

How it works

Take the digit 4 of Tag 4127, the first digit in the figure. It has 28 × 28 = 784 numbers. Of these, 664 are 0, which is 664 / 784 = 0.85 of the picture, and the other 784 − 664 = 120 are greater than 0.

28 × 28rows times columns=784numbers in the digit|664 ÷ 784the share that is 0=85%empty paper

A plain network, one built from the neurons of Part B, reads the digit as a list of 784 numbers. A neuron in its first layer multiplies them by 784 weights of its own and adds the products. Reordering the pixels and the weights in the same way leaves this sum unchanged.

Common belief. A network that reads pictures must know which pixels are neighbours.

Why it fails. A small plain network (128 hidden ReLU units) was trained once on the 60,000 normal training digits and once on digits shuffled by one fixed rule. On the 10,000 test digits, shuffled in the same way, the second network classified 97.0% correctly, against 96.9% for the first. The 0.1 point gap is within the noise of a single run, so shuffling did not visibly hurt.

Better account. A plain network does not build in the layout of the pixels. A convolution does: it applies the same few weights to small patches all over the picture, as the rest of this chapter shows.

Quick quiz

The digit 7 of Tag 4127 has 668 zeros among its 784 numbers. What share is that, and how many numbers are not 0?

The share is 668 / 784 = 0.85, which is 85%, and 784 − 668 = 116 numbers are not 0. Most of the picture is empty paper, and the other numbers lie along the pen path.

Why can a plain network learn from shuffled digits when you cannot read them?

Its first layer multiplies the pixels by weights of their own and adds the products. Reordering the pixels and the weights in the same way leaves the sum unchanged, so the layout of the pixels is not part of the arithmetic.

Terms

pixel
one square of the grid, holding one number
grey value
the number in a square: 0 is no ink, 255 is full ink
array
a grid of numbers with a size such as (28, 28) (0.1)
flatten

Reading the figure

Hover over, or tap, any square and read its number. Squares are counted by row from the top, then by column from the left, so the top-left square is row 0, column 0. A file stores a value in one byte, which allows 256 values, 0 to 255. Machine learning code usually divides by 255 so that values lie between 0 and 1. This chapter keeps 0 to 255 because those numbers are easier to read. The digits come from MNIST, a public set of 70,000 handwritten digits. Tag 4127 is four digits: 4, 1, 2 and 7. Switch to Add ink and draw on the grid. The count of zeros changes as you go.

The shuffle test

Now tick Shuffle the squares. All squares move to new places, by one fixed random rule, and you can no longer read the digit. A plain network from B1 and B2 is not bothered. It reads a digit as a list of 784 inputs and gives all of them separate weights. It does not use which squares are neighbours. A network with 784 inputs, 128 ReLU units and 10 outputs was trained for 5 passes over the 60,000 training digits, once on normal digits and once on shuffled ones. On the 10,000 test digits it classified 96.9% and 97.0% of them correctly. That is one run per case, and the 0.1 point gap is within the noise of a single run.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. Arrays are indexed image[row, column], which is [y, x]. If a digit looks mirrored along its diagonal, you swapped the two. Also check the scale: a model trained on values from 0 to 1 that receives values from 0 to 255 sees inputs 255 times too big. Print image.max() before you feed an image to a model.

Colour is three grids

Guess first. A photo of a hammerhead shark is 640 pixels wide and 362 high. How many numbers does it need? And when the same scene is photographed 10 m under the surface, which colour do you expect to lose first: red, green or blue?

A channel is a grid of numbers for one colour of light, and a colour photo has three: red, green and blue (RGB). A pixel is therefore three numbers, and a photo of 640 × 362 pixels has 640 × 362 × 3 = 695,040 numbers. Water absorbs red light faster than green and blue light, so red is the colour lost first.

  1. Move the pointer over any of the four pictures: the box under them reads that pixel as three numbers, red, green and blue.
  2. Drag Depth to 10 m. This applies the depth model of the domain-shift chapter to the same photo: the red grid turns almost black, and the boxes show the mean red falling and the mean blue rising.
  3. Set Filter size to 3 by 3 and Number of filters to 16: the last box counts 448 numbers to learn.

At 10 m the mean red of the hammerhead photo falls from about 51 to about 7, while the mean blue rises from about 153 to about 170.

How it works

A filter is a small grid of weights that slides over a picture; on a colour photo it needs a weight for all three channels of the patch under it. For a 3 by 3 filter that is 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 weights. It also has one bias, a number added to its result, so one filter has 28 numbers to learn. A layer of 16 such filters has 28 × 16 = 448 numbers.

3 × 3 × 3weights of one filter+1bias=28numbers in one filter×16filters=448numbers to learn

A layer has \((k \cdot k \cdot C_{\text{in}} + 1)\, C_{\text{out}}\) parameters, the numbers it learns. Here \(k\) is the side of the filter and \(C_{\text{in}}\) is the number of channels the layer reads (3 for an RGB photo). \(C_{\text{out}}\) is the number of filters, and \(+1\) is the bias of one filter.

Common belief. Deeper water makes a photo darker and no other change.

Why it fails. In the depth model of the figure the three grids change differently. At 10 m the mean red is about 13% of its surface value, while the mean green rises from about 78 to about 111 and the mean blue from about 153 to about 170. The model adds haze, which is scattered blue-green light, and a simulated automatic exposure that brightens a dark picture.

Better account. Water changes the balance between the channels as well as the brightness, so a model trained on surface photos receives inputs with different ranges.

Quick quiz

How many numbers has one 5 by 5 filter that reads an RGB photo, with its bias?

The count is 5 × 5 × 3 = 75 weights, plus 1 bias, so 76 numbers.

The photo doubles in width and height. Does a filter get more numbers?

No. The count \((k \cdot k \cdot C_{\text{in}} + 1)\, C_{\text{out}}\) has no width or height in it. The same 76 numbers of a 5 by 5 filter slide over a small or a large photo.

Terms

channel
one grid of numbers for one primary colour; a grey picture has one channel, a colour picture three
RGB
red, green and blue, as three grids with values 0 to 255
bias
one more number added to the result of a filter

Array sizes and the figure

The hammerhead photo has 640 × 362 × 3 = 695,040 numbers. In NumPy the array has size (362, 640, 3), with the channel last. PyTorch wants the channel first: (3, 362, 640). A grey digit is the same thing with one channel. Untick a channel to see what the photo looks like without it. At depth 10 m the green grid also looks brighter. In the depth model this comes from the haze and the simulated automatic exposure, not from extra green light from the shark.

The figure draws the photo at half its width, 320 by 181 pixels, so the row and column in its pixel readout count in that smaller copy. The domain-shift chapter follows what a different range in the three channels does to a classifier.

Symbols and the ResNet-18 example

\[ \text{parameters} = \left(k \cdot k \cdot C_{\text{in}} + 1\right)\, C_{\text{out}} \]

  • \(k\) is the side of the filter in squares, so a window has \(k \cdot k\) squares.
  • \(C_{\text{in}}\) is the number of channels the layer reads (3 for an RGB photo).
  • \(C_{\text{out}}\) is the number of filters, which is also the number of feature maps the layer writes.
  • The \(+1\) is the bias of one filter.

The boxes above the credit line work it out for the sliders. With the default choices, 3 by 3 and 16 filters, the layer has (27 + 1) × 16 = 448 numbers, whatever the size of the photo. The first layer of ResNet-18 (used in C3) reads RGB with 7 by 7 filters and writes 64 maps. It has 7 × 7 × 3 × 64 = 9,408 weights. It has no biases because a batch-norm layer (B6) follows.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. If a blue shark looks orange, the channels are in the wrong order. OpenCV reads pictures as blue, green, red, while PIL and PyTorch use red, green, blue. Swap with image[:, :, ::-1] and check one pixel you know.

A filter slides over the picture

Guess first. The left-right edge filter is a 3 by 3 grid of weights. From top to bottom its rows are −1, 0, 1 and −2, 0, 2 and −1, 0, 1. What does it output over a patch where all nine pixels have the same value? And at the left edge of a pen stroke, where the picture goes from paper to ink?

A filter (or kernel) is a small grid of weights. At one position its window, the patch of pixels under it, gives one output: the dot product of the window with the weights, the sum of the nine products of matching numbers. The filter repeats this at all positions, so its outputs form a grid, the feature map, which is large and positive where the window looks like the pattern in the weights.

  1. Press Play, or click the digit to place the window: the feature map fills in as the window slides. The boxes show the nine pixels under the window, the weights, the products and their sum.
  2. With Edge left-right, teal (positive) marks windows with paper on the left and ink on the right, because the right column has the positive weights; coral (negative) marks the reverse; flat paper gives 0.
  3. Click Edge top-bottom, then Blur, and compare the maps.

Input, 28 by 28. Click to move the window.

Feature map, 26 by 26. Coral is below 0, teal above 0.

The left-right edge filter gives 0 on a flat patch and a large value at an edge: on this digit the outputs reach +1010 and −1010.

How it works

The figure starts with the window whose output has the largest absolute value, at row 14, column 18. The window has ink on its left and paper on its right, and its rows are 252, 167, 0 and 253, 107, 0 and 252, 106, 0.

−252top row: −1·252 + 0·167 + 1·0+−506middle row: −2·253 + 0·107 + 2·0+−252bottom row: −1·252 + 0·106 + 1·0=−1010output, negative: ink on the left

The feature map has the value \(O[i,j] = \sum_{u=0}^{k-1}\sum_{v=0}^{k-1} K[u,v]\, I[i+u,\, j+v] + b\) at row \(i\), column \(j\). Here \(K[u,v]\) is the weight at row \(u\), column \(v\) of a filter of side \(k\), \(I\) is the picture, and \(b\) is the bias (0 in the figure). A dot product is large when two lists rise and fall together, so the output is large where the window varies like the weights. The edge filter's weights add up to 0, so a flat window of value \(c\) gives \(c \times 0 = 0\).

Analogy. A filter is a stencil that you slide over a page, asking at any spot how well the page matches it.

Where it breaks. A stencil answers yes or no, while a filter gives a graded number that can be negative. In a convolutional network the weights are usually not designed: they start random and gradient descent adjusts them.

Quick quiz

A sharpen filter has weights 0, −1, 0 / −1, 5, −1 / 0, −1, 0. What does it output on a flat window of value 100?

The output is 5 × 100 − 4 × 100 = 100. The weights add up to 1, so a flat window gives its own value back and only differences from the neighbours are boosted.

If all weights of the edge filter changed sign, what would it output on the worked window?

It would output +1010. The output is a sum of products, so changing the sign of all weights changes the sign of the sum, and −(−1010) = 1010.

Terms

filter (kernel)
a small grid of weights, 3 by 3 here
window
the patch of squares under the filter at one position
feature map
the grid of filter outputs, one per position
dot product
multiply matching numbers and add them up (0.5)

The presets

Pick the presets in turn. Edge left-right subtracts the left column from the right column and counts the middle row twice. Its weights add up to 0, so a flat patch gives 0. Edge top-bottom does the same with rows. Blur gives all nine squares the weight 1/9, so the output is their average. Sharpen gives the middle weight 5 and its four neighbours −1, which keeps the middle value and adds the difference from its neighbours. Identity copies the middle square. Then type your own nine numbers. Tick then ReLU to keep only the positive outputs, which is what many networks do after a filter (B1).

The feature map is 26 by 26, smaller than the 28 by 28 input, because a window must fit inside the picture. The next section gives the rule. An output is one dot product of the window with the weights. By the dot product of 0.5, the result is large when the window points the same way as the weights and has large values. So the map has large values where the picture looks like the pattern in the weights.

Symbols

\[ O[i,j] \;=\; \sum_{u=0}^{k-1}\sum_{v=0}^{k-1} K[u,v]\; I[i+u,\; j+v] \;+\; b \]

  • \(I[r,c]\) is the input value at row \(r\), column \(c\), and \(O[i,j]\) is the feature-map value at row \(i\), column \(j\).
  • \(K[u,v]\) is the filter weight at row \(u\), column \(v\) inside the window. Its side is \(k\) (3 in the figure). Here \(K\) is short for kernel, the filter. It does not mean the keys of attention (D4).
  • \(b\) is a bias added to all outputs of the filter. The figure uses \(b = 0\).
  • The two sums run over the \(k \cdot k\) squares of the window: nine products, then one total.

A second worked example

Take a window that is dark on the left and bright on the right: all rows are 0, 0, 255. This is a second worked example, for the edge filter and for the blur.

255top row: −1·0 + 0·0 + 1·255+510middle row: −2·0 + 0·0 + 2·255+255bottom row: −1·0 + 0·0 + 1·255=1020edge filter output
3 × 255the nine squares add up to this÷9squares in the window=85blur output

A flat window with all nine values equal to 128 gives 0 under the edge filter, because the weights add up to 0 and 128 × 0 = 0. Under the blur it gives 128. That answers the guess-first question: 0 on a flat patch, a large number at an edge. The largest possible output of this edge filter is 1020, which is 4 × 255. The colour scale of the map is set by the largest absolute value in the map, so it changes with the filter and the digit. The status line under the maps gives it as the value of full colour.

Where it works and where it breaks

The filters in the figure are made by hand, so that you can see what a pattern of weights does.

When it works and when it breaks. One set of nine weights is reused at all positions, so a pattern is found wherever it appears and the filter needs only nine numbers. It does respond to one pattern in one size and orientation. The left-right filter says little about a horizontal stroke (switch to top-bottom and compare). A network therefore uses many filters at once. Libraries call this operation convolution, but strictly it is cross-correlation: the kernel is not flipped. A true convolution flips the kernel first. For the left-right edge filter the flip changes the sign of the output. For a learned filter it makes no difference to what the network can represent, because training can find whichever version is needed.

A weight used at all positions collects the slopes from all of them (B4, a value used twice).

Common mistakes

Debug tip. Test a convolution on a tiny picture whose answer you can work out by hand, then compare with a library. A picture with a dark left half and a bright right half should give a band of large values where the halves meet (two columns for a 3 by 3 filter), and 0 elsewhere.

In Python

import numpy as np

def conv2d(image, kernel, stride=1, pad=0):
    image = np.pad(image, pad)                      # zeros around the edge
    k = kernel.shape[0]
    n = (image.shape[0] - k) // stride + 1          # output size
    out = np.zeros((n, n))
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(n):
            window = image[i * stride : i * stride + k, j * stride : j * stride + k]
            out[i, j] = np.sum(window * kernel)     # sum of products
    return out

image = np.zeros((6, 6)); image[:, 3:] = 255        # dark left half, bright right half
edge = np.array([[-1, 0, 1], [-2, 0, 2], [-1, 0, 1]])
mine = conv2d(image, edge)
print(mine)
[[   0. 1020. 1020.    0.]
 [   0. 1020. 1020.    0.]
 [   0. 1020. 1020.    0.]
 [   0. 1020. 1020.    0.]]

The two columns of 1020 come from the windows that straddle the boundary between the dark and bright halves. A check against PyTorch's own convolution (not runnable in the browser) confirms the function:

import torch, torch.nn.functional as F
ref = F.conv2d(torch.tensor(image)[None, None], torch.tensor(edge, dtype=torch.float64)[None, None])[0, 0].numpy()
print("same as PyTorch:", np.allclose(mine, ref))
same as PyTorch: True

More questions

Why does the edge filter need weights that add up to 0 to give 0 on flat patches?

On a flat patch all nine values equal one number c, so the output is c times the sum of the weights. That is 0 only if the weights sum to 0.

Stride and padding

Guess first. A 28 by 28 digit goes through a 3 by 3 filter, moving one pixel at a time. How big is the feature map? And what could you add around the picture so that the map stays 28 by 28?

The window can move by \(s\) pixels between positions, where \(s\) is the stride, and \(p\) rings of zeros, the padding, can be added around the picture. For an input of side \(n\) and a filter of side \(k\), the feature map has side \(m = \lfloor (n + 2p - k)/s \rfloor + 1\). The brackets \(\lfloor\ \rfloor\) round down to a whole number. Padding makes the map bigger because it adds \(2p\) to the width, and stride makes it smaller because the window skips positions.

  1. The left grid is the input (n = 7) and the right grid is the output. Click an output square to see its window; small dots mark the window's top-left corners.
  2. Drag Padding p to 1: dashed squares of zeros appear around the input, and the output grows to 7 by 7 because the window now fits at 7 positions along a side.
  3. Set Padding p back to 0 and drag Stride s to 2: the window jumps two pixels at a time, so the output shrinks to 3 by 3.

With s = 1 and p = 0 the map is 5 by 5; p = 1 makes it 7 by 7, and s = 2 (with p = 0) makes it 3 by 3.

How it works

For the 28 by 28 digit with k = 3 and s = 1, the formula gives 26 when p = 0 and 28 when p = 1. The arithmetic is (28 + 0 − 3)/1 + 1 = 26 and (28 + 2 − 3)/1 + 1 = 28. With p = 1 and s = 2 the quotient is 27/2 = 13.5, the floor drops the half step, so the side is 13 + 1 = 14.

26p = 0|28p = 1|14p = 1, s = 2 (27 ÷ 2 floors to 13)

Padding makes the width \(n + 2p\). The window's top-left corner can be at 0, \(s\), \(2s\) and so on, up to \(n + 2p - k\), the last position where the window fits. The number of steps of size \(s\) that fit is \(\lfloor (n + 2p - k)/s \rfloor\), and the starting position adds 1.

Common belief. A stride of 2 only makes the map smaller. It still reads all pixels of the picture.

Why it fails. Set n = 8, k = 3, s = 2, p = 0 and tick Count how often a square is read. The last row and column are crossed out: 15 pixels are never read, because the quotient 5/2 = 2.5 is rounded down.

Better account. If \(s\) is at most \(k\) and divides \(n + 2p - k\), all pixels are read; otherwise some pixels can stay unread.

Quick quiz

What padding keeps a 5 by 5 filter at stride 1 from changing the size?

The output side equals \(n\) when \((n + 2p - 5)/1 + 1 = n\), so \(2p - 4 = 0\) and \(p = 2\). In general \(p = (k-1)/2\) for odd \(k\).

A 3 by 3 filter with stride 2 and no padding reads a 10 by 10 picture. How big is the output, and which pixels are never read?

\(\lfloor (10 - 3)/2 \rfloor + 1 = \lfloor 3.5 \rfloor + 1 = 4\). The windows start at columns 0, 2, 4 and 6, and the last one ends at column 8, so column 9 is never read, and likewise row 9.

Terms

stride \(s\)
how many squares the window moves between positions; 1 moves one square at a time
padding \(p\)
rings of zeros added around the picture before sliding
output size \(m\)
the number of window positions along one side of the picture; here \(m\) is not the number of examples

Symbols

\[ m \;=\; \left\lfloor \frac{n + 2p - k}{s} \right\rfloor + 1 \]

  • \(n\) is the side of the input, in squares. \(p\) is the number of rings of zeros added on all four sides.
  • \(k\) is the side of the filter and \(s\) is the stride.
  • \(m\) is the side of the output, not the number of examples. The brackets \(\lfloor\ \rfloor\) round down to a whole number.
  • With a stride the sum reads from \(I[s\,i + u - p,\ s\,j + v - p]\), so a step of \(i\) moves the window by \(s\) squares and the \(-p\) puts the padding rings at negative positions.

Same padding and a larger example

A map of the input's size is usually called “same” padding. For odd \(k\) and \(s = 1\) it needs \(p = (k-1)/2\).

The first layer of ResNet-18 reads a 224 by 224 photo with \(k = 7\), \(s = 2\), \(p = 3\): \(\lfloor 223/2 \rfloor + 1 = 111 + 1 = 112\).

112ResNet-18, n = 224, k = 7, s = 2, p = 3

How often a square is read

Play with the four sliders and watch the equation boxes. When the stride is larger than the filter, whole columns between windows are skipped. Adding padding changes \(n + 2p - k\) and so changes the leftover strip at the far edge. The zeros of the padding are the first squares in that strip, so a leftover of at most \(p\) squares drops only padding.

Tick Count how often a square is read. With the starting sliders (\(n = 7\), \(k = 3\), \(s = 1\)) and \(p = 0\), the corner squares are read once and the centre squares nine times. A pen stroke at the border can therefore have less influence than one in the middle. With a ring of padding the corner count rises to 4. Zero padding is a choice: where the picture is not 0 at its border, the zeros add an artificial edge, and edge filters respond along the border.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. A common error in a first CNN is a size mismatch after Flatten: the dense layer expects a different number of inputs than the last feature map provides. Work the sizes out with the formula, or print x.size() after the layers, before you write the dense layer.

In Python

def out_size(n, k, s=1, p=0):
    return (n + 2 * p - k) // s + 1    # // rounds down

print(out_size(28, 3), out_size(28, 3, p=1), out_size(28, 3, s=2, p=1))
print(out_size(224, 7, s=2, p=3), out_size(11, 2, s=2), out_size(100, 7, s=3))
26 28 14
112 5 32

The same sizes from PyTorch layers, plus the count of numbers in a layer with 16 filters from the previous section:

import torch, torch.nn as nn
x = torch.zeros(1, 3, 224, 224)
print(nn.Conv2d(3, 64, kernel_size=7, stride=2, padding=3)(x).shape)
print(sum(p.numel() for p in nn.Conv2d(3, 16, 3).parameters()))
torch.Size([1, 64, 112, 112])
448

More questions

A 2 by 2 pool with stride 2 reads an 11 by 11 map. How big is the output, and what happens to the last row and column?

\(\lfloor (11 - 2)/2 \rfloor + 1 = 5\). The last row and the last column of the map are never read.

Max pooling

Guess first. You move the digit one pixel to the right and recompute the feature map: by about what share does the map change? Then you cut the map into 2 by 2 blocks and keep only the largest value in a block. Does the smaller map change by more, by the same share, or by less?

Pooling replaces a block of the feature map by one number. Max pooling keeps the largest value in a block of side \(q\) and does not record where in the block it was. Max pooling shrinks the map because a block of \(q \times q\) values becomes one value, and in the figure it makes the map less sensitive to small shifts of the digit.

  1. With the starting choices, drag Move the digit to the right, in squares to 1. The readout shows the change of the map: the length of the difference between the maps of the moved and original digit, as a share of the length of the original map. It is 95% before pooling and 68% after.
  2. Hover over the pooled map: the coral square on the left map marks the block, and the line below shows its four values and their maximum.
  3. Drag the slider to 3: the pooled map still changes by 132%, against 141% unpooled.

Feature map after the filter and ReLU, 26 by 26

After pooling

Max pooling halves the width and height of the map and lowers the change from a one-pixel shift of this digit from 95% to 68%, but does not remove it.

How it works

With the slider at 0, hover over the pooled map at output row 9, column 7. Its block has the values 543, 1009, 510 and 1010, so the maximum is 1010. The block to its right has the maximum 500. When the digit moves one pixel to the right, the strong values 1009 and 1010 enter the right block, so the two maxima become 543 and 1010.

max(543, 1009, 510, 1010the block) =1010pooled value|after the move: max(0, 543, 0, 510the same block) =543pooled value

The pooled value at row \(i\), column \(j\) is \(P[i,j] = \max_{0 \le u,\,v < q} F[s\,i + u,\; s\,j + v]\). Here \(F\) is the feature map before pooling, \(P\) the pooled map, \(q\) the side of the block and \(s\) the stride between blocks. The output side follows the formula of the last section with \(k\) replaced by \(q\) and \(p = 0\), so a 26 by 26 map with \(q = s = 2\) becomes \(\lfloor 24/2 \rfloor + 1 = 13\) by 13.

Common belief. Pooling makes a network recognise a digit wherever it is in the picture.

Why it fails. At a shift of 3 pixels, more than the two-pixel width of a block, the pooled map of this digit still changes by 132%, against 141% before pooling.

Better account. Pooling tolerates small shifts that keep the strongest value inside its block.

Quick quiz

A 13 by 13 map goes through 2 by 2 max pooling with stride 2. What size is the result?

\(\lfloor (13 - 2)/2 \rfloor + 1 = 6\). The last row and column are not read.

Why does a move of 3 pixels still change the pooled map?

A block is 2 pixels wide, so a move of 3 pixels puts all strong values in different blocks than before. The block maxima then change, and for this digit the pooled map changes by 132%, against 141% before pooling.

Go deeper 30-digit averages, symbols, costs, Python about 3 min

Terms

pooling
replace a block of the map by one number
max pooling
keep the largest value in the block
average pooling
keep the mean of the block
pool size \(q\)
the side of the block; stride is the step between blocks

Averages over 30 digits

The figure shows one digit. Averaged over the 30 MNIST digits of the figure's data, with the left-right edge filter, moving the digit one pixel to the right changes the feature map by 88% of its own size, and the 2 by 2 max-pooled map by 65%. A likely reason is that the strongest value of a block often stays inside the same block when the pattern moves one pixel. At a move of 3 pixels the averages are 139% before pooling and 128% after. Here the change is the square root of the sum of the squared differences between the two maps, divided by the square root of the sum of the squared values of the original map.

Symbols

\[ P[i,j] \;=\; \max_{0 \le u,\,v < q}\; F[\,s\,i + u,\; s\,j + v\,] \]

  • \(F\) is the feature map before pooling and \(P\) the pooled map; \(q\) is the block side and \(s\) the stride.
  • Here \(F\) is a feature map. The Fisher information of B7 has the same letter and a different meaning.
  • For average pooling replace the maximum by the mean of the \(q \cdot q\) values. Pooling has no weights to learn.

What pooling costs

Larger tolerance to shifts can come from stacking several conv and pool layers and from training on shifted examples.

What pooling costs. It throws away the position inside a block. That is fine when you want to know that a stroke exists. It hurts when the position is the answer, for example the distance between a shark's eye and its tail fin. Many modern networks use a stride-2 convolution instead of a pooling layer, so the network learns what to keep. ResNet-18 has one max pool near the start and averages over the whole map at the end.

The next chapter stacks the filters, strides, padding and pooling of this chapter into a network that reads the digit, and measures that network on shifted digits (where it fails).

Common mistakes

Debug tip. If you pool an odd-sized map, the last row and column are dropped, as in the 11 to 5 example. When that matters, pad the map first or change the sizes. Also remember that max pooling passes the slope back only to the square that held the maximum (B4).

In Python

A tiny map shows both sides of the tolerance. The 9 and the 8 are strong responses of a filter.

import numpy as np

def maxpool(m, q=2, s=2):
    n = (m.shape[0] - q) // s + 1
    return np.array([[m[i*s:i*s+q, j*s:j*s+q].max()
                      for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)])

m = np.zeros((4, 4), int); m[0, 1] = 9; m[2, 3] = 8   # two strong responses
for shift in (0, -1, 1):          # no move, one square left, one right
    pooled = maxpool(np.roll(m, shift, axis=1))
    same = bool((pooled == maxpool(m)).all())
    print(f"shift {shift:2d}:", pooled.tolist(), "same as before:", same)
shift  0: [[9, 0], [0, 8]] same as before: True
shift -1: [[9, 0], [0, 8]] same as before: True
shift  1: [[0, 9], [8, 0]] same as before: False

Moving the map one square left keeps both maxima inside their blocks, so the pooled map is the same. Moving it one square right pushes both into another block (np.roll wraps the 8 around to the left edge), and the pooled map changes.

    0  0  200 200 200
0  0  200 200 200
0  0  200   0 200
0  0  200 200 200
0  0  200 200 200
    Hint

    The centre window is the 3 by 3 block with the missing bright square in its middle. Write the nine values in a grid first, then multiply by the weights.

  2. theory Find the output side for these layers. (a) \(n = 32\), \(k = 5\), \(s = 1\), \(p = 2\). (b) \(n = 100\), \(k = 7\), \(s = 3\), \(p = 0\). (c) \(n = 28\), \(k = 3\), \(s = 2\), \(p = 0\). Which squares of the input are never read in (b) and (c)?

    Hint

    Compute \(n + 2p - k\) first. The squares never read are at the end of the picture, where the last window stops.

  3. theory A convolution layer reads a 28 by 28 grey digit and writes 6 feature maps with 3 by 3 filters. How many numbers does it learn, and how many does a dense layer need to produce the same 6 maps of 26 by 26 from the 784 inputs? Why do the two counts differ so much?

  4. theory Show that for a filter whose weights add up to 1, a flat window of value \(c\) gives \(c\). Then show that scaling all weights by 2 doubles all outputs.

Practice

  2. practice Use depth.py to make the hammerhead photo at 0, 5, 10 and 20 m. For the depths print the mean of the red, green and blue grids. At what depth does the mean red fall below 10% of the mean blue?

Think deeper

  1. open You want a 3 by 3 filter that finds the horizontal bar of a 7 and one that finds its diagonal stroke. What weights would you try, and how would you test them on the digits? What goes wrong when a digit is written slightly larger?

  2. open SharkCam wants to measure how long a shark is in the picture. Max pooling forgets position inside a block. Where in a network could that hurt this measurement, and what would you do instead?

  3. open Under water the red grid has little information. How would you test how much a channel helps a shark classifier? What could go wrong with your test, for example if the photos come from different cameras?

Come back later

Try these after two days and again after a week. Say the answer aloud before you open it.

A neuron from B1 computes \(z = \mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x} + b\). What is a 3 by 3 filter at one position, and how does it differ from that neuron?

It is the same sum: the nine pixels in the window play the part of \(\mathbf{x}\), the nine filter weights are \(\mathbf{w}\), and \(b\) is the bias. The difference is reuse. The filter applies the same weights at all positions, so nine numbers produce a whole map. A plain neuron would need separate weights for separate positions.

The dive camera takes a photo at 10 m and the red grid is almost empty. In B6, batch norm stores a mean and a variance per channel. Why might those stored numbers be wrong for this photo?

They were measured on training photos taken near the surface, where red is bright. At 10 m the red values, and so the first layer's outputs for them, are much smaller. The stored mean and variance no longer describe the inputs, so the normalised values are off. C3 follows this idea.

A 3 by 3 conv layer with padding 1 reads 12 maps of size 13 by 13 and writes 24 maps. What size are the outputs and how many numbers does the layer learn?

Same size, 13 by 13, because \(p = (k-1)/2\). Parameters: \((3 \cdot 3 \cdot 12 + 1) \cdot 24 = 109 \cdot 24 = 2{,}616\).
